tagline: Four freeways meet at Farmington Hills’ southwest corner, and the freight bound for the Novi and Wixom distribution corridor passes through them every day. When one of those trucks causes a crash, the carrier, the trailer’s owner, and sometimes the shipper are part of the case.

c.v: At Farmington Hills’ southwest corner, I-696 ends and I-96, I-275, and M-5 meet in a single interchange. It is the junction where freight moving between Detroit, Lansing, Grand Rapids, the airport cargo terminals, and the northern suburbs changes freeways, and where trucks bound for the distribution and light-industrial corridor in Novi and Wixom leave I-696 for I-96. Inside the city, box trucks and tractor-trailers serve the office and engineering campuses on Twelve Mile and Halsted, the retail on Orchard Lake Road and Grand River, and the light-industrial parks off Haggerty and Halsted. In 2024, according to the Michigan State Police, 2,081 heavy trucks and buses were involved in crashes in Oakland County, and 110 people were killed and 3,613 injured in heavy truck and bus crashes statewide.

A truck crash is not a car crash with a larger vehicle. The driver and the carrier are governed by federal safety regulations whose violation is evidence of negligence. The carrier must hold $750,000 or more in insurance. The records that prove the case, the driver’s electronic logs and the truck’s engine data, can be lawfully discarded within months, and the carrier’s insurer will have an investigator on the case within days. sections.heading: Where Farmington Hills truck crashes happen

c.v: The interchange.

I-696, I-96, I-275, and M-5 meet in one interchange with ramps to Twelve Mile, Orchard Lake, Grand River, and Haggerty. Trucks changing freeways here cross lanes of traffic doing the same in the other direction. The crashes are merge and weave collisions on the ramps and the short connectors between them; trucks changing lanes into a car in the blind spot on the right side of the cab; rear-end and underride crashes in the stop-and-go on I-696 west of Orchard Lake and on I-96 at the Novi line; and rollovers on curved ramps when a truck takes them too fast or its load shifts (49 CFR Part 393).
I-96 and I-275 toward Novi and Wixom.

I-96 west of the interchange carries freight to the distribution centers, suppliers, and light industry along the Novi and Wixom corridor, and I-275 carries it south toward I-94 and the airport. Rush-hour congestion meets trucks running delivery appointments, which is where hours-of-service pressure and following-distance cases come from.
Grand River, Orchard Lake, and Twelve Mile.

Delivery trucks serving the Grand River and Orchard Lake retail strips, the hospital on Grand River, and the office campuses on Twelve Mile and Halsted: wide right turns across two lanes, trucks backing into docks and service drives from the road, trucks stopped in a travel lane waiting to enter, and trucks pulling out into fast traffic. On a boulevard with Michigan lefts, a tractor-trailer cannot always make the crossover in one movement, and a truck stalled across a crossover or swinging wide into the far lanes is a recurring hazard. When a facility’s dock layout or delivery schedule puts trucks in the road, the facility or its logistics provider may share responsibility with the carrier.
The light-industrial parks.

Off Haggerty, Halsted, and Eleven and Twelve Mile, trucks turning into and out of industrial driveways and backing at loading docks injure drivers of smaller vehicles, cyclists, pedestrians, and the workers at the docks themselves (see our
pedestrian accident page
Whose road it is.

I-696, I-96, I-275, M-5, and Grand River, including the interchange ramps, are MDOT’s; a road-defect claim against the State goes to the Court of Claims, with written notice filed there within 120 days (MCL 691.1404). Orchard Lake, Haggerty, Halsted, Middlebelt, Inkster, Farmington Road, and the mile roads, including Eight Mile, are generally the Road Commission for Oakland County’s, and subdivision streets the City of Farmington Hills’, with 120 days’ notice (MCL 691.1404).

sections.heading: Who is responsible, and who pays

c.v: The carrier, not just the driver.

The motor carrier is responsible for its drivers’ compliance with the Federal Motor Carrier Safety Regulations and is liable for a driver’s negligence in the course of employment. Michigan applies the federal rules to intrastate carriers (MCL 480.11a), so a local hauler running between Oakland County suppliers is held to the same standards as an interstate carrier. The rules that decide truck cases most often:

c.v: The owner of the truck or trailer.

In Michigan, a vehicle’s owner is liable for its negligent operation by someone driving with the owner’s consent (MCL 257.401). When the tractor, the trailer, and the driver belong to different companies, which is common in freight, each may be a defendant, although a company in the business of renting or leasing vehicles is generally shielded from owner liability by federal law (49 USC 30106).
Michigan no-fault still applies to you.

Your own auto insurer pays your medical bills, 85 percent of lost wages up to the monthly cap DIFS sets each year, replacement services, and attendant care regardless of fault (MCL 500.3107), with written notice due within one year (MCL 500.3145(1)). The Michigan Assigned Claims Plan pays if no household policy applies (MCL 500.3172). Your claim against the driver and the carrier for pain and suffering and losses beyond no-fault requires a threshold injury (MCL 500.3135) and must be filed within three years (MCL 600.5805(2)). That claim includes wage loss above the no-fault cap or beyond three years (MCL 500.3135(3)(c)), which for many Farmington Hills professionals is a large part of the loss. If you were more than 50 percent at fault, you cannot recover pain-and-suffering damages, and below that your share reduces them (MCL 500.3135(2)(b)). The difference from a car case is the money available: the carrier’s $750,000-plus policy, often with excess coverage above it. See our
no-fault insurance claim page
Other defendants.

The shipper or broker that loaded the trailer or hired an unsafe carrier; the facility or logistics provider whose dock operations contributed; the maintenance contractor; the manufacturer of a failed component (
product liability
); and, for a government truck (City of Farmington Hills, the Road Commission, MDOT, SMART), the agency under the motor vehicle exception to governmental immunity (MCL 691.1405).
If you were the truck driver.

Workers’ compensation pays your benefits, and your employer usually cannot be sued (MCL 418.131). If you were injured in your employer’s truck, no-fault benefits generally come from the insurer of that truck (MCL 500.3114(3)), coordinated with comp, which is paid first (MCL 500.3109(1)). You can also sue a third party, such as another driver or a facility whose dock operation caused the crash. See our
Farmington Hills workers’ compensation page

sections.heading: The evidence, and how fast it disappears

c.v: Carriers must keep hours-of-service records for six months (49 CFR 395.8) and driver inspection reports for three months (49 CFR 396.11); after that the regulations no longer require them. MDOT freeway cameras at the interchange, business and campus cameras along Grand River, Orchard Lake, and Twelve Mile, and dash cameras overwrite in days to weeks. The truck’s engine control module and event data recorder can be cleared when it is repaired and returned to service.
The first act in a Farmington Hills truck case is a
preservation letter

: to the carrier, its insurer, the tractor and trailer owners, the shipper or broker, and, where the crash happened at or near a facility, the facility and its logistics provider. It demands the ELD and engine data, dash camera footage, the driver’s qualification file and post-crash test results, dispatch records and bills of lading, dock appointment and arrival logs, maintenance files, and the truck itself for inspection. Once a party knows a claim is coming, destroying that evidence exposes it to spoliation sanctions.

faqs.question: How many truck accidents happen in Farmington Hills?

answer.v: The State’s county profile does not break out truck crashes by city. Countywide, 2,081 heavy trucks and buses were involved in Oakland County crashes in 2024, and statewide 15,888 crashes involved a heavy truck or bus.

faqs.question: A semi changed lanes into me at the I-696/I-96 interchange. Who is at fault?

answer.v: Usually the driver who changed lanes into an occupied lane. A tractor-trailer has large blind spots on its right side, and the driver must check them before moving over. The truck’s engine data, dash camera, and MDOT’s freeway cameras show what happened, which is why they have to be preserved quickly.

faqs.question: I was rear-ended by a truck in I-696 traffic. Who pays?

answer.v: Your own no-fault insurer pays your medical bills and lost wages first, regardless of fault. The carrier’s insurer pays for pain and suffering and losses beyond no-fault, including wages above the no-fault cap, once a threshold injury is established.

faqs.question: A delivery truck was blocking a lane on Grand River and I hit it. Is that my fault?

answer.v: Not necessarily. Following too closely is usually the claim against the rear driver, but a truck stopped in a travel lane without warning, or a business whose delivery schedule routinely puts trucks in the road, can carry fault too. The cameras and the truck’s data decide it.

faqs.question: I drive a truck and was hurt in a crash in Farmington Hills. What are my claims?

answer.v: Workers’ compensation through your employer, no-fault benefits coordinated with comp, and a lawsuit against any third party who caused the crash.

faqs.question: Why does the lawyer need to act within days?

answer.v: Because the records expire: six months for hours-of-service logs, three months for inspection reports, days or weeks for camera footage, and the truck’s electronic data can be cleared on repair.

faqs.question: Is a truck case worth more than a car case?

answer.v: The injuries are usually worse and the insurance is usually larger: a $750,000 minimum for a general freight carrier, against $50,000 for a minimally insured car.
